pg:https://kotaku.com/zelda-ocarina-of-t.desc: Fans still want Zelda on a cartridge
paras: Physical games are dying, unless your game is called The Legend of Zelda. The Switch 2 remake of Ocarina of Time just sold 1 million physical copies in its first week in the U.S., the most of any release since Tears of the Kingdom released in 2023.

Nintendo previously announced that Ocarina of Time sold 5.2 million copies globally across physical and digital in its first four days, which blew the original game’s debut on Nintendo 64 out of the water. It’s a wild number when you consider it’s a Switch 2 exclusive. The newest Nintendo console has only been out for roughly 18 months and only has an install base of around 26 million units, making the attach rate for the game nearly one in five.

There are, of course, two ways to take the Ocarina of Time remake’s physical game sales milestone. The first is to see it as a sign of how strong Switch 2 owners’ attachment to cartridge-based gaming remains even as digital swallows most of the market for game sales. The other is to note that no other game has managed to sell 1 million physical copies in the U.S. within its first week in over three years.

pg:https://www.ign.com/articles/the-lege.desc: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake is running rampant on PC, but can Nintendo actually do anything about it? We asked legal experts to find out.
paras: Shortly after the release of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake, players quickly found ways to start playing it on PC.

This was done through a few different methods. One is through an emulator, whereas others are through recompilation tools, which run the game natively on PC without emulating the Switch 2. Either way, the people who make these emulators and tools insist that users have to supply their own game files, so the downloads won’t work on their own. In other words, they want you to buy the game before you start playing it on PC, to cover their backs.

This is nothing new for a big release, but we’ve never seen it done so quickly before. That’s because many of these emulators and tools were AI-assisted, which is also why you have seen so many other “native” PC ports of games floating around (to mixed results — and fears concerning how safe they actually are to play).

pg:https://www.videogameschronicle.com/n.desc: It’s the first game to sell 1 million physical copies in week one in the US since Tears of the Kingdom…
paras: Video Game News 17th Nov 2026 / 9:24 am Posted by Chris Scullion The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake has become the best-selling physical game in the US this year, after just its first week on sale.
As reported by Circana senior director Mat Piscatella, the Ocarina of Time remake sold more than 1 million physical copies in the US in its first week on sale.
This made it the best-selling physical game of the year in the US so far, with no other physical release managing to cumulatively sell all year what Ocarina managed in one week.

The Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake for Switch 2 got off to an outstanding start, selling over five million copies (approx 5.2 million units) in just four days. Sales in the UK and Japan have contributed to this, and now, Circana Retail Tracking Service has shared data about the title's US launch.

As highlighted by Circana's senior director and video game industry advisor Mat Piscatella (via social media), "after just one week", Ocarina of Time for Switch 2 is this year's "best-selling physical video game in the US". Interestingly, it's the first title to surpass one million physical units in a US launch week since the 2023 Switch title, The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom.

Considering the year is almost over, and Grand Theft Auto 6's retail release is actually a "code-in-box", we imagine Ocarina's remake will hold onto the title of 2026's best-selling physical game (that's actually a proper physical game). However, there is one technicality - Circana tracks and reports "code-in-box" sales as "new physical video game sales", so Zelda may not actually keep the crown. paras: Few things in cinema are more subjective than deciding who was the best, or worst, James Bond. The same goes, broadly speaking, for choosing between actors who have played the same character. Such debates can lead to lively and fiercely contested arguments... except in obvious cases such as Superman (Christopher Reeve) and, to open another can of worms, Batman (George Clooney, though he was saddled with the worst suit and the worst script in the worst film).

There have been several James Bonds. By the official canon, there have been seven actors in the role, although an eighth, David Niven, played him in the 1967 Casino Royale, a film made outside the Eon Productions umbrella, the company that held the screen rights to Ian Fleming’s creation. pg:https://www.cbc.ca/news/science/voyag.desc: Voyager 1, already the farthest a human-made object has ever gone, has crossed the arbitrary but important threshold of a light day. It now takes 24 hours to send a message to the probe, now in interstellar space.
paras: Launched in 1977, Voyager 1 was meant to study the gas giants of our solar system, Jupiter and Saturn. But by 1998, it continued on past them, becoming the farthest human-made object ever. It reached interstellar space — the region just outside the sun’s magnetic influence known as the heliopause — back in 2012, at a distance of 18 billion kilometres. Now, it’s more than 26 billion kilometres away.

Arguably, being a “light day” away is an arbitrary threshold, as there’s no new physical boundary or change to Voyager 1 itself. But experts say it’s remarkable because it’s still plugging along on its mission while communicating with Earth.

Voyager 1’s power is generated by the heat from the natural decay of plutonium. As that power has dwindled over nearly half a century, most of its science instruments have been shut down, the latest being the LCEP, which measured low-energy charged particles. There are two instruments that still work, one for measuring plasma waves and the other for magnetic fields.

paras: NASA Add Engadget on Google: Google Discover If NASA's estimates are correct, Voyager 1 is already one light-day away from our planet. NASA expects it to have reached that milestone at 5:16:07 AM Eastern time today, November 18. One light-day is the distance a particle of light can travel in a day. Since radio waves travel at the speed of light, it now takes 24 hours to send a command to the probe and 24 hours to get a message back. That's why NASA won't be able to confirm exactly what time it reached one light-day away until tomorrow, when the probe's message arrives.

Voyager 1 headed to space in 1977 as part of NASA's program to study not just our Solar System, but also interstellar space. It was launched 16 days after Voyager 2, but it has since traveled farther than its twin and any other probe we've sent out. Voyager 1 reached interstellar space — that's the region between star systems — back in 2012, before Voyager 2 did. It suffered technical glitches, and NASA had to shut down some of its features to keep it going despite the diminishing plutonium in its generator. But it's still around and hasn't stopped its journey.

After traveling for 49 years, two months and 11 days, it's now believed to be about 16 billion miles from our planet—and it's not done yet. Voyager 1 is headed toward a star called Gliese 445, about 17 light-years from Earth in the Ursa Minor constellation. In terms of space distances, that's not so far away. However, none of us would be here by the time it reaches that goal: It's expected to pass within 1.7 light-years of Gliese 445 in 40,000 years.

According to NASA's calculations, the milestone occurred at 5:16:07 a.m. Eastern Time on Wednesday. One light-day is the distance a particle of light can travel in 24 hours, equivalent to about 26 billion kilometers.

Launched in 1977 to fly by Jupiter and Saturn, Voyager 1 has been traveling through space for nearly 50 years. paras: The United Nations’s top court has found Myanmar guilty of “genocidal intent” in massacres that killed 10,000 Rohingya in its military operations in 2017.

The International Court of Justice (ICJ) at The Hague delivered its judgement on Thursday over the military crackdown that drove more than 730,000 mainly Muslim Rohingya to flee to neighbouring Bangladesh.

The case was brought by the West African nation of The Gambia, which in 2019 accused Myanmar of seeking to destroy the Rohingya people.
